fields.name: ah
fields.label: Battery capacity
fields.hint: From the battery label. Common sizes are 100, 150 and 200 Ah.

fields.name: load_w
fields.label: Load
fields.hint: Total watts the battery is powering. For a fridge or cooler use its average draw, not the peak.

fields.name: inverter_eff
fields.label: Inverter efficiency
fields.hint: As a decimal. Enter 1 for a DC load wired straight to the battery.

fields.name: idle_w
fields.label: Inverter idle draw
fields.hint: What the UPS or inverter uses itself, even with nothing plugged in (no-load current × battery volts on its label). Not counted when inverter efficiency is one (a DC load).

fields.name: dod
fields.label: Usable depth of discharge
fields.hint: As a decimal: 0.5 means half the battery. Leave blank to use the value for your battery type.

answer: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery runs a {{in.load_w|int}} W load through an inverter for about {{out.hours|hm}}, using only the {{out.dod|pct}} of its capacity that is safe to use. Runtime in hours equals Ah × volts × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw); for a DC load set the efficiency to one.
how: {{in.ah}} Ah × {{in.volts|1}} V × {{out.dod|pct}} usable = {{out.stored_wh|int}} Wh in the battery. The battery gives {{in.load_w}} W ÷ {{out.inverter_eff|pct}} inverter efficiency + {{out.idle_w}} W the inverter draws itself = {{out.battery_w|1}} W. {{out.stored_wh|int}} Wh ÷ {{out.battery_w|1}} W = {{out.hours|2}} hours, about {{out.hours|hm}}. Battery current: {{out.battery_w|1}} W ÷ {{in.volts|1}} V = {{out.battery_a|1}} A, {{out.c_rate|2}} times the battery's Ah (its C-rate), rising to {{out.cutoff_a|1}} A as the battery nears its low-battery cut-off; the cables and fuse must carry that.
key_facts: Runtime of a {{in.volts|int}} V battery in hours = Ah × {{in.volts|int}} V × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw).

A {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery stores about {{out.stored_wh|int}} Wh of usable energy, which through an inverter runs a {{in.load_w|int}} W load for about {{out.hours|hm}} or a {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W load for about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}}.

Lead-acid, AGM and gel batteries should be used to about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} of their rating; lithium (LiFePO4) batteries to about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}}, so a lithium battery of the same Ah runs almost twice as long.

An inverter running at about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} efficiency turns the rest of the battery energy into heat; the inverter also draws about {{data.appliances.ups-idle.running_w|int}} W itself while it is on. A DC load wired straight to the battery has neither loss.

lines: Ah = battery capacity in amp hours
η = inverter efficiency (1 for a DC load)
P_idle = the inverter's own draw with no load (from its label; none for a DC load)

sections.h2: How long will a {{in.volts|int}} V battery run a {{in.load_w|int}} W load?
p: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah, {{in.volts|int}} V lead-acid battery runs a {{in.load_w|int}} W AC load for about {{out.hours|hm}} through an inverter. The same load wired as DC, with no inverter, runs longer, because there is no inverter loss (about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} efficiency) and no idle draw of the inverter itself. A {{ex.2.in.ah|int}} Ah lithium battery at {{ex.2.in.volts|1}} V stores about {{ex.2.out.stored_wh|int}} Wh usable, so it runs the same {{in.load_w|int}} W load for roughly twice as long.

The result does not depend on your mains voltage. Whether the inverter puts out {{d.v_1ph|int}} V as in Pakistan, the UK and Europe, or {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V as in the US and Canada, the battery side is the same {{in.volts|int}} V and the watts drawn are the same.

sections.h2: {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery runtime calculator: lead-acid against lithium
p: The label Ah is not the usable Ah. A {{in.ah|int}} Ah lead-acid, AGM or gel battery should only be taken to about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} of its rating, so only half the energy counts. A {{in.ah|int}} Ah lithium (LiFePO4) battery can safely use about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}}, and sits at {{ex.2.in.volts|1}} V instead of {{in.volts|int}} V, which is why the lithium example below gives about {{ex.2.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W while a lead-acid battery of the same Ah gives much less.

Lead-acid batteries also lose capacity when they are drained fast. The label Ah is measured over about twenty hours; at a load that empties the battery in an hour the real capacity can be a quarter lower. The calculator does not apply this drop, so treat results under about two hours as optimistic.

mistakes: Using the full Ah. A lead-acid battery taken below about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} loses cycles quickly, so only that part counts as usable.
Forgetting the inverter. An inverter turns about {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} of the battery energy into AC; leave the efficiency at one only for a true DC load.
Using the fridge's peak watts. A fridge compressor cycles on and off; use the average draw over a day or the runtime will look far too short.
Trusting the label Ah at high loads. Lead-acid capacity is rated over about twenty hours; a load that empties the battery in an hour or two gets noticeably less.
Mixing up a car battery with a deep cycle battery. A car starting battery is built for short bursts and is damaged by deep discharge, so set a smaller depth of discharge for it.
safety: Fuse the battery cable close to the battery, size the cable for the inverter current, keep lead-acid batteries ventilated, and have a licensed electrician connect any inverter to house wiring.

faq.q: How long will a {{in.volts|int}} V battery last?
faq.a: Divide the usable watt-hours by what the inverter takes from the battery: the load watts ÷ its efficiency, plus its own idle draw. A {{in.ah|int}} Ah lead-acid battery has about {{out.stored_wh|int}} Wh usable, so it lasts about {{out.hours|hm}} at {{in.load_w|int}} W, about {{ex.4.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.4.in.load_w|int}} W if it is a {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah battery, and about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W.

faq.q: A {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery gives how many hours?
faq.a: About {{out.hours|hm}} at {{in.load_w|int}} W through an inverter, or about {{ex.2.out.hours|hm}} at {{ex.2.in.load_w|int}} W if it is a {{ex.2.in.volts|1}} V lithium battery. The hours fall almost in proportion as the load rises.

faq.q: Can a {{in.volts|int}} V {{in.ah|int}} Ah battery run a {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W load?
faq.a: Only briefly: about {{ex.1.out.hours|hm}} on paper, and less in practice because a lead-acid battery drained that fast delivers less than its label Ah. You also need an inverter rated for the load and a thick, fused battery cable for the high current.

faq.q: Is this a {{in.volts|int}} V battery life calculator?
faq.a: It calculates runtime on one charge, not the life of the battery in years. Battery life depends on how deep and how often you discharge; staying within about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} for lead-acid and about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} for lithium is what makes a battery last.

faq.q: How long will a {{in.volts|int}} V battery run a fridge?
faq.a: Use the fridge's average draw, not its peak. A {{ex.3.in.volts|int}} V compressor fridge averaging about {{ex.3.in.load_w|int}} W runs about {{ex.3.out.hours|hm}} on a {{ex.3.in.ah|int}} Ah lead-acid battery wired as DC. A mains fridge through an inverter draws more and also pays the inverter loss.

faq.q: What is the runtime of a {{in.volts|int}} V deep cycle battery?
faq.a: The same formula applies; deep cycle batteries are simply built to be taken to about {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} repeatedly. A {{ex.4.in.ah|int}} Ah deep cycle battery runs a {{ex.4.in.load_w|int}} W load for about {{ex.4.out.hours|hm}} through an inverter.

faq.q: How do I work out the discharge time of a {{in.volts|int}} V battery?
faq.a: Discharge time in hours = Ah × {{in.volts|int}} V × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw). For a DC load drop the inverter efficiency and the idle draw; then usable Wh ÷ watts gives the hours and Ah × depth of discharge ÷ amps gives the same answer.
